children: By Sara Randazzo
Can a law firm partner dramatically increase their value simply by moving to a competitor?
That’s a bet many law firms are making these days, as it becomes almost routine for the most profitable firms to pay star recruits $20 million or more.
But the firms making those investments have their own data suggesting the hires don't always pan out.

When legal consultant Blane Prescott, who helps law firms set compensation, asked a room full of managing partners a few years ago what percentage of their lateral partners met financial projections in the first year, the average answer was 20%. It only rose to 30% by the end of the second year.
“It’s hard,” Prescott said, likening it to the high number of marriages that end in divorce.

I’ve been trying to understand the calculus that goes into offering partners athlete-level sums, and what I’ve learned from talking to recruiters, lawyers and consultants is that it’s sometimes grounded in reputation and aspirations as much as hard numbers.

As an elite tier of firms competes for the biggest names and clients, some I spoke to wondered if the compensation race is leading firms to take risks they wouldn’t have in the past. The high pay is also putting pressure on partners to immediately prove their worth at a new firm. Those who don’t live up to the promises can see their pay cut or be asked to leave, but firms don’t want to get in the habit of making bad decisions.
“The rules are just flying out the window,” Los Angeles-based recruiter Naomi Kaplan said of how she's seeing compensation being set now versus in the past.
THE $20 MILLION QUESTION

One of the latest $20 million men in Big Law is Christopher Machera, who left a role as co-head of Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ private equity practice for the partnership at New York-based Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison. People familiar with the move said he’ll be getting at least $20 million at Paul Weiss. Machera didn’t return a request for comment.

Every few weeks brings news of another splashy hire as partners switch firms in dizzying numbers. More than 2,000 partners moved between the nation’s 200 highest-grossing law firms in the first half of the year — a new record, and a 55% increase since 2021 — according to legal analytics firm SurePoint.

Even firms that traditionally haven't poached much from competitors are jumping in, like Cravath, Swaine & Moore announcing Friday it hired a team of M&A partners from Weil, led by prominent dealmaker Michael Aiello.

As Karen Andersen, a recruiter at Major, Lindsey & Africa sees it, law firms are looking for transformational hires whose reputations will help each side accomplish more than they could have on their own. The pitch, she says, is: “We can make something bigger.”

Even with due diligence, new hires can often disappoint. Legal intelligence firm Decipher finds that 51% of new-partner hires leave within five years, 64% fail to deliver their promised business and 36% never fully integrate. Decipher, which helps law firms vet lateral hires, also found that 40% of lateral partner candidates last year prompted concerns about their business development claims or client relationships, including whether clients would actually follow them to a new firm.

The risks have done little to deter top firms, which are benefiting from a surge in revenue. Driven by rising billing rates and increased demand, the 200 highest-grossing firms posted a 12.4% increase in revenue in the first half of the year, compared to the same period last year, according to Wells Fargo's Legal Specialty Group.

Prescott said the factors he sees driving partner pay ever-higher include the impact of annual rate increases, the ballooning size and complexity of corporate deals and jury verdicts, and an overemphasis at some firms on tying a partner's compensation to which client relationships they initiated. Tallying such origination credit can lead to selfishness, Prescott and others told me, and inflate the amount of work claimed by top rainmakers.
All together, the factors mean that, “These days, you see people who legitimately have $80 million to $100 million worth of work that follows them,” Prescott said.

Such numbers can justify partner pay of $20 million and up, at firms including Latham & Watkins; Kirkland & Ellis; Paul Weiss; Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan; Paul Hastings; and others. At a rarefied few, some partners make $30 million or even $40 million a year. The firms declined to comment or didn't respond to requests.
MIND THE GAP

The ever-increasing pay at the top is the latest sign of law firms' long-running transformation from traditional partnerships into businesses that increasingly resemble corporations. Most firms have eliminated practices like paying purely by seniority and valuing less-tangible contributions like leadership as much as revenue-generation.

The gap also continues to grow between the highest and lowest paid partners within a firm. A few decades ago, firms hesitated to go beyond a 3-to-1 or 4-to-1 ratio between highest and lowest paid, lest it breed too much envy.

Now, such numbers look quaint.  At Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher, for instance, a recruiter tells me equity partner pay now ranges from less than $2 million to $28 million, a spread of at least 14 to 1. At some firms, the range is even wider. Gibson Dunn declined to comment.

Even for those Gibson equity partners on the low end of the scale, I'd say $2 million isn't so bad. That it can make someone look underpaid inside an elite law firm says a lot about how much the industry has changed.
